newsitem.title: USA: Pro-Israeli group's critics hail U.S. court ruling.
newsitem.headline: Pro-Israeli group's critics hail U.S. court ruling.

text.p: Opponents of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee on Monday hailed a court ruling that could make the pro-Israeli group subject to federal campaign law regulation.

The opinion on Friday by the U.S. Court of Appeals in Washington reversed a finding by the Federal Election Commission that AIPAC was not a political organisation under the legal test the agency had used.
As a political organisation, AIPAC would have to make regular reports on its contributions to the election commission and to limit those contributions to no more than $1,000 per candidate.

The election commission ruled in 1992 that AIPAC was not subject to its regulation because its political activities were not its major purpose. A federal judge and then a three-judge panel of the appeals court upheld the ruling.

But the full appeals court, in an 8-2 decision, overturned the earlier rulings, saying the elections agency improperly applied the "major purpose" test. It sent the case back to the FEC for further review.

"This decision is the beginning of the end to the stranglehold that the Israeli lobby has had on U.S. Middle East policy," former U.S. Information Agency official Richard Curtiss said in a statement. He was one of six individuals whose lawsuit against the election commission led to the ruling.
Other plaintiffs included former U.S. ambassador to Saudi Arabia James Akins and former congressman Paul Findley, who says AIPAC helped defeat him for re-election in 1982.
"Now AIPAC will be held to the same standard that less powerful political lobbies must meet," Curtiss added.
Judge Lawrence Silberman, who wrote the majority opinion, said the FEC misinterpretated the law in deciding AIPAC was not a political organisation.

"The FEC's interpretation of 'political committee' would allow a large organisation to contribute substantial sums to campaign activity, as long as the contributions are a small portion of the organisation's overall budget, without being subject to the limitations and requirements imposed on political committees," Silberman wrote.
The FEC could appeal the decision to the U.S. Supreme Court. An FEC spokesman said attorneys for the commission were studying the opinion.

AIPAC officials said they were waiting to see what the commission did since their organisation was not a defendant in the suit. But they expressed confidence the FEC would again find that AIPAC was not a political organisation under different legal grouds.
